First tone + first tone: both high and level.
First tone + second tone: stay high, then rise.
First tone + fourth tone: stay high, then fall.
Fourth tone + first tone: fall, then jump back up high.
Second tone + first tone: rise, then stay high.
Second tone + third tone: rise, then go low.
Second tone + fourth tone: rise, then fall.
Third tone + first tone: stay low, then jump up high.
Third tone + second tone: stay low, then rise.
Third tone + fourth tone: stay low, then fall from high.
Fourth tone + second tone: fall, then rise.
Fourth tone + third tone: fall, then stay low.
Fourth tone + fourth tone: two falls, the second one stronger.
First tone + neutral tone: the second syllable is short and light.
Fourth tone + neutral tone: fall, then a light, short xie.
From 水 (water). As in 汤 (tāng, soup) and 河 (hé, river).
From 人 (person). As in 你 (nǐ, you) and 他 (tā, he).
At the bottom of a character. As in 想 (xiǎng, to think) and 您 (nín, you, polite).
心 standing on the left. As in 怕 (pà, to be afraid) and 忙 (máng, busy).
Short form of 言 (speech). As in 说 (shuō, to speak) and 谢 (xiè, to thank).
From 手 (hand). As in 打 (dǎ, to hit; to play) and 找 (zhǎo, to look for).
On top, from 草 (grass). As in 花 (huā, flower) and 茶 (chá, tea).
From 食 (food). As in 饭 (fàn, meal) and 饿 (è, hungry).
As in 地 (dì, ground) and 城 (chéng, city).
From 金 (gold). As in 钱 (qián, money) and 铁 (tiě, iron).

added: Putting a syllable together

Now put the pieces together. A syllable is an initial, a final and a tone: 来 is l + ai + the second tone, lái (to come). The tone mark sits on a or e if the final has one, on the o of ou, and otherwise on the last vowel: duì, niú. The cards below are common one-syllable words. Read the pinyin aloud before you flip each card, and find its initial, final and tone.

added: Strokes

Characters are made of strokes: lines, dots and hooks. There are only a few basic strokes, and every character is built from them. Knowing them helps you see the parts and look characters up. This course does not drill stroke order.

StrokeWhat it looks likeSeen in
horizontala line from left to right一, 三
verticala line straight down十, 中
left-fallinga sweep down to the left人, 八
right-fallinga sweep down to the right, thick at the end人, 八
dota short dab六, 氵
turna line that bends at a corner口, 日
hooka flick at the end of a line小, 子

removed: The oldest characters began as drawings. 人 rén is a person walking, 口 kǒu an open mouth, 木 mù a tree with roots, 山 shān three peaks, 日 rì the sun and 月 yuè the moon.
added: The oldest characters began as drawings. 人 rén is a person walking, 口 kǒu an open mouth, 木 mù a tree with roots, 山 shān three peaks, 日 rì the sun and 月 yuè the moon. More pictures: 女 nǚ is a woman, 子 zǐ a child with its arms out, 门 mén a door, 雨 yǔ rain falling, 火 huǒ a flame and 水 shuǐ a stream. 上 shàng (up) and 下 xià (down) are a mark above and below a line.
Radicals: hints, not spellings

A radical is the part of a character that hints at its meaning. Many radicals are picture characters, squeezed to one side. Three dots on the left (氵) mean water, as in 汤 tāng (soup). A small 口 on the left often marks a mouth word or a sound. 亻, a narrow form of 人, means a person, as in 你 nǐ (you). 女 means a woman.
Here are the radicals you will meet most. A tile shows the pinyin of the full character the radical comes from: 讠 is a short form of 言 yán (speech), and 忄 is 心 xīn (heart) standing on the left.
{{tiles:zh.tl004}}

Another part often hints at the sound. 妈 mā (mom) is 女 (woman) for the meaning and 马 mǎ (horse) for the sound. The hint is rough: you cannot sound out a character letter by letter, so learn each one with its pinyin.

added: Most characters are built from two or three parts you already know. Sometimes every part gives the meaning, as in 好. More often the radical gives the meaning and the other part gives the sound: 请 qǐng (please), 清 qīng (clear) and 晴 qíng (sunny) all take their sound from 青 qīng, and 讠 (speech), 氵 (water) and 日 (sun) tell them apart.
